title: Two-photon: going deep
objective: Explain why two-photon excitation images deeper and localizes excitation.

steps.title: Two low-energy photons, one event
steps.body: **[[two-photon microscopy|Two-photon]]** excites a fluorophore only where two infrared photons arrive almost simultaneously — which only happens at the tight focal point. Infrared light also scatters less in tissue, so two-photon reaches deeper and excites *only* the focal volume.

steps.prompt: Why does two-photon cause less out-of-focus damage than confocal?
options: Excitation happens only right at the focal point
Its infrared photons each carry more energy
It scans faster, so each spot gets less light
Its confocal pinhole is substantially larger
steps.explanation: Only the focal volume gets enough photon density to excite, so planes above and below aren't bleached or damaged.

variants.setup: You focus a two-photon laser deep inside a thick sample.
variants.prompt: Where does it actually excite the dye?
options: Essentially only at the focal point
variants.reveal: Two-photon excitation is confined to the focus, sparing other planes.

steps.setup: You want to image calcium activity hundreds of microns deep in a living brain.
steps.reveal: Infrared penetrates deeper with less scatter, and localized excitation suits living tissue — two-photon is the standard for deep in vivo imaging.

variants.prompt: Deep in vivo calcium imaging usually uses…
variants.explanation: IR depth + localized excitation make two-photon ideal in vivo.

reviewNotes: Two-photon; forward-ref to calcium imaging in C11.
